issues.legal_issue: A tenant cannot deduct or adjust repair expenses against rent when the tenant's claim to recover those expenses is barred by limitation.
material_facts: A tenant claimed that amounts spent on repairs to rented premises should be adjusted against rent arrears.
The claim to recover some of the repair expenses had become barred by limitation.
issues.conclusion: Repair expenses that the tenant can no longer recover because of limitation cannot be adjusted against rent due.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 20 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rents Act, 1957, as explained in Maganlal v. Chandrakant, deduction is a mode of recovery; when recovery by suit is barred, recovery by deduction is barred as well. The same principle applies to adjustment of repair expenses against rent, since it would be anomalous for one mode of recovery to remain available after the other is barred.

predicates.landlord_tenant_rent_arrears_case: A landlord brought a proceeding to recover rent arrears from a tenant.
predicates.tenant_repair_cost_claim_time_barred: A tenant sought to recover repair expenses, but the claim for those expenses was barred by limitation.
predicates.time_barred_repair_cost_cannot_be_set_of: A tenant cannot apply repair expenses that are no longer recoverable against rent due.

issues.definition: When a tenant's repair-cost claim is time-barred in a rent-arrears proceeding, those costs cannot be used to reduce the rent due.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant's claim for the cost of repairs paid to third parties, where the landlord had no obligation to pay those third parties, is governed by the general residual limitation rule rather than the rule for money paid for a defendant.
material_facts: The tenant paid third parties for repairs to the rented premises, including repairs undertaken after notice to the landlord.
The landlord had no statutory or contractual obligation to pay the third parties for the repairs.
The courts below disagreed over whether the claim for repair expenses was subject to a three-year or six-year limitation period.
issues.conclusion: The rule for money paid for a defendant did not apply; the claim was governed by Article 113 read with Section 30 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and the six-year limitation period applied. After adjustment of the timely repair expenses, the tenant was not in arrears for more than six months and was not liable to eviction for default.
issues.legal_principle: Article 23 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to money paid for a defendant and, by necessary implication, requires that the defendant be legally obliged to pay a third party. Because the landlord had no statutory or contractual liability to the repairers, the tenant's payments were not made for the landlord. Article 113 read with Section 30 therefore governed the claim, and the Court agreed with the High Court that the six-year limitation period applied.
